# String Comparison Methods
## Concepts Creating Strings Using String Literals Using `new` Keyword Comparing Strings using Equality (`==`) Operator Strings Comparison Methods equals() equalsIgnoreCase() compareTo() compareToIgnoreCase() Comparing Characters
## Introduction In the previous units, we have learned about working with strings such as creating strings, comparing strings using the equality operator(`==`), etc. In this unit, we will explore more ways to create and compare strings in Java. To get started, let's learn how strings are actually created in Java, and then we will learn how to compare the strings using different string methods.
## 1. Creating Strings In Java, strings can be created in two ways: 1. Using string literal 2. Using `new` keyword ### 1.1 Using String Literals A string literal is a value which is enclosed in double quotes (`" "`). In Java String literal is created by using double quotes. #### Example ```java String str = "ABC"; ``` Here, `"ABC"` is a string literal which is assigned to the variable `str`. In Java, when the strings are created using string literals with the same value, both the strings point to the same reference. As a result, memory can be saved during the execution of the code. ### 1.2 Using `new` Keyword A string can be created by initializing the `String` class with the `new` keyword. #### Syntax ```java String str1 = new String(str); ``` Here, `str` is a string literal (example: "ABC"). When a string is created using the `new` keyword, the string is stored in a new memory location. Now, let's see how these strings are compared in Java
## 2. Comparing Strings In Java, we can make comparisons between two strings in different ways. Some of them are listed below. - Using Equality (`==`) operator - Using `equals()` method - Using `equalsIgnoreCase()` method - Using `compareTo()`method - Using `compareToIgnoreCase()` method ### 2.1 Using Equality (`==`) Operator Using the `==` operator, we have already learned how to compare strings. It compares the strings based on their memory locations. _Example 1:_ #### Code ```java class CompareStrings { public static void main(String[] args) { String str1 = "ABC"; String str2 = "ABC"; System.out.println(str1 == str2); } } ``` #### Output ``` true ``` In the above example, `str1` and `str2` are created using a string literal and they both have the same value so both the strings will have the same reference. As, the equality operator compares the strings based on the reference, the above code prints `true`. _Example 2:_ #### Code ```java class CompareStrings { public static void main(String[] args) { String str1 = new String("ABC"); String str2 = new String("ABC"); System.out.println(str1 == str2); } } ``` #### Output ``` false ``` In the above code, as `str1` and `str2` are created using the `new` keyword, both the strings will be pointing to different memory locations. So, using the equality operator for comparing the strings that are created using `new` keyword returns `false` eventhough both strings have the same value. Therefore, the equality operator can only be used when comparing strings that are created using string literals and it cannot be used for strings created with the `new` keyword Let's look at string comparison methods to compare strings created with the `new` keyword.
## 3. String Comparison Methods ### 3.1 equals() The `equals()` method is used to check if the given string is equivalent to another string. It returns `true` if the given strings are equal. Otherwise `false` is returned. The `equals()` method differentiates between cases, i.e, it is case-sensitive. #### Syntax ```java str1.equals(str2); ``` #### Code ```java class CompareStrings { public static void main(String[] args) { String str1 = "ABC"; String str2 = "ABC"; String str3 = new String("ABC"); String str4 = new String("ABC"); System.out.println(str1.equals(str2)); System.out.println(str3.equals(str4)); System.out.println(str1.equals(str3)); } } ``` #### Output ``` true true true ``` ### 3.2 equalsIgnoreCase() The `equalsIgnoreCase()` works similar to the `equals()` but ignores the case difference between the strings. It returns `true` if the given strings are equal. Otherwise `false` is returned. #### Syntax ```java str1.equalsIgnoreCase(str2); ``` #### Code ```java class CompareStrings { public static void main(String[] args) { String str1 = "ABC"; String str2 = "abc"; String str3 = new String("aBc"); System.out.println(str1.equalsIgnoreCase(str2)); System.out.println(str1.equalsIgnoreCase(str3)); } } ``` #### Output ``` true true ``` >
> **Comparison with Python** >
> > _Example 1:_ > > #### Code > > ```python > print("ABC" == "ABC") > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > > True > ``` > > _Example 2:_ > > #### Code > > ```python > print("ABC" == "abc") > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > > False > ``` > > As Python is case-sensitive the strings "ABC" and "abc" are not equal. > >

### 3.3 compareTo() The `compareTo()` method is used to compare two strings based on the Unicode values. For each corresponding character of the strings, the calculation will be, `character of first string` \- `character of second string` (operation is based on the Unicode values). The `compareTo()` method is case-sensitive. #### Syntax ```java str1.compareTo(str2); ``` Here, - if `str1` == `str2`, it returns `0` - if `str1` > `str2`, it returns **positive** number - if `str1` < `str2`, it returns **negative** number _Example 1:_ #### Code ```java class CompareStrings { public static void main(String[] args) { String str1 = "ABC"; String str2 = "ABC"; System.out.println(str1.compareTo(str2)); } } ``` #### Output ``` 0 ``` _Example 2:_ #### Code ```java class CompareStrings { public static void main(String[] args) { String str1 = "A"; String str2 = "B"; System.out.println(str1.compareTo(str2)); } } ``` #### Output ``` -1 ``` In the above example, the `compareTo()` method internally evaluates `65 - 66 = -1`. So, the output is `-1`. It means that `str1` is less than `str2` _Example 3:_ #### Code ```java class CompareStrings { public static void main(String[] args) { String str1 = "AB"; String str2 = "AA"; System.out.println(str1.compareTo(str2)); } } ``` #### Output ``` 1 ``` In the above example, the `compareTo()` method internally evaluates, - First characters: `65 - 65 = 0` - Second characters: `66 - 65 = 1` so, the output is `1` ### 3.4 compareToIgnoreCase() The `compareToIgnoreCase()` works similar to the `compareTo()` but ignores the case difference between the strings. #### Syntax ```java str1.compareToIgnoreCase(str2); ``` Here, - if `str1` == `str2`, it returns `0` - if `str1` > `str2`, it returns **positive** number - if `str1` < `str2`, it returns **negative** number #### Code ```java class CompareStrings { public static void main(String[] args) { String str1 = "AbC"; String str2 = "aBc"; System.out.println(str1.compareToIgnoreCase(str2)); } } ``` #### Output ``` 0 ```
## 4. Comparing Characters Similar to Python, we can compare characters using relational operators such as `==`, `>` and `<` in Java. _Example 1:_ #### Code ```java class CompareCharacters { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println('A' < 'B'); } } ``` #### Output ``` true ``` The Unicode value of `A` is `65` and `B` is `66`, which internally compares as `65 < 66`. So the output is `true` >
> **Comparison with Python** > > #### Code > > ```python > print("A" < "B") > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > > True > ``` > >

_Example 2:_ #### Code ```java class CompareCharacters { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println('P' >= 'Q'); System.out.println('H' == 'H'); } } ``` #### Output ``` false true ```
### Summary - Creating strings: - Using string literals allocates the same memory location when strings with the same value are created. - Using the `new` keyword allocates a different memory location for every string created. - Methods to compare strings: - `equals()`: It returns `true` if the given strings are equal. Otherwise `false` is returned. - `equalsIgnoreCase()`: It works similar to `equals()`, but ignores the case difference between the strings. - `compareTo()`: It is used to compare two strings. For each corresponding character of the strings, the comparison takes place based on the Unicode values. It returns an integer value. - `compareToIgnoreCase()`: It works similar to the `compareTo()` but ignores the case difference between the strings. - Using the relational operators, we can compare characters based on their Unicode values.

# More Arithmetic Operations
## Concepts Math Class pow() round() DecimalFormat Class Floating Point Errors
## Introduction In the previous units, we learned arithmetic operators to perform basic mathematical computations. In addition, we will learn some built-in math methods available in the `Math` class in order to perform more mathematical operations and how to write comments in Java. ## 1. Math Class The Java `Math` class provides different methods for performing mathematical operations such as exponentiation, rounding off, etc. The `Math` is located in `java.lang` package so it need not be imported. Let's look at some of its methods. - `pow()` - `round()` ### 1.1 pow() The `pow()` method is similar to `**` operator in Python. It accepts two numbers and returns the value of the first number raised to the second number (exponentiation). It returns a `double` type of value. #### Syntax ```java Math.pow(base, exponent); ``` Here, the `base` and `exponent` should be of `double` type. **Key Points:** - If the second parameter is zero then the result will be `1.0`. - When we pass an `int` value to the `pow()` method, it implicitly converts the `int` value to a `double` value. _Example:_ #### Code ```java class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { int base = 6; int exponent = 3; double result = Math.pow(base, exponent); System.out.println(result); } } ``` #### Output ``` 216.0 ```
>
> **Comparison with Python** > > #### Code > > ```python > print(6 ** 3) > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > > 216 > ``` > >

### 1.2 round() The `round()` method rounds the specified value to the closest `int` or `long` value. #### Syntax ```java Math.round(num); ``` Here, `num` is the number that is to be rounded (should be `float` or `double` type) - It returns the `int` value if the argument is `float` - It returns the `long` value if the argument is `double` _Example 1_: **`round()` with `float` value** #### Code ```java class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { float floatNum = 10.53f; int rounded = Math.round(floatNum); System.out.println(rounded); } } ``` #### Output ``` 11 ``` In the above code, as the `float` type is passed to the `round()` method, it returned the `int` value. _Example 2_: **`round()` with `double` value** #### Code ```java class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { double doubleNum = 5.654d; long rounded = Math.round(doubleNum); System.out.println(rounded); } } ``` #### Output ``` 6 ``` In the above code, as the `double` type is passed to the `round()` method, it returned a `long` value. >
> **Comparison with Python** > > #### Code > > ```python > num = round(3.14, 1) > print(num) > num = round(3.14) > print(num) > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > 3.1 > 3 > ``` > > In Python, we can use round(number, digits(optional)) to round float values to the given decimal digits. In Java, the `round()` method accepts only one parameter. > >
But, the `round()` cannot be used to round to certain decimal places, it always rounds to the nearest integer.
## 2. DecimalFormat Class The `DecimalFormat` class from the package `java.text` used to format decimal numbers. #### Syntax ```java DecimalFormat df = new DecimalFormat("#.###"); df.format(num); ``` Here, - `df` is the variable name (object of `DecimalFormat`). - `#` after the decimal point indicates how many decimal digits we are rounding off to. - `num` is the number to be rounded off. Initially, we need to create a _DecimalFormat_ object and then call the `format()` method of that object to round off the given numbers. The `format()` method takes a `double` or `long` value and returns a `String` value If `float` or `int` are data types are passed, they are implicitly converted to `double` and `long` respectively. #### Code ```java import java.text.DecimalFormat; class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { double doubleNum = 1.666; DecimalFormat df = new DecimalFormat("#.##"); System.out.println(df.format(doubleNum)); } } ``` #### Output ``` 1.67 ```
## 4. Floating Point Errors In Java, float values are stored approximately in the same manner as in Python. Sometimes, floating-point approximation gives unexpected results. let's check it with an example, #### Code ```java class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2); System.out.println((0.1 + 0.2) == 0.3 ); } } ``` #### Output ``` 0.30000000000000004 false ``` In the above code, we can see that `0.1 + 0.2` is evaluated as `0.30000000000000004`. Hence, comparing this value with `0.3` resulted in `false`. >
> **Comparison with Python** > > #### Code > > ```python > print(0.1 + 0.2) > print((0.1 + 0.2) == 0.3) > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > 0.30000000000000004 > False > ``` > >
### Summary - The `Math` class provides many methods for performing mathematical operations. - `pow()`: It calculates the exponents and returns the result. - `round()`: It rounds the specified value to the closest `int` or `long` value and returns it. - The `DecimalFormat` class from the package `java.text` used to format decimal numbers.

## Introduction

In the previous units, we have learned arithmetic operators, relational operators, logical operators, etc.

In this unit, we will learn some more commonly used operators such as compound assignment operators, and increment and decrement operators

## 1. Compound Assignment Operators

Compound assignment operators provide a shorter way to assign an expression to a variable. These operators are also known as Shorthand Assignment Operators.

There are different compound assignment operators available in Java: `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=`, etc.

The Compound Assignment Operators in Java works similar to those in Python

![](https://s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/new-assets.ccbp.in/frontend/content/java/java-rm-compound-assignment.webp)

_Example 1:_

```java
class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
       int a = 5;
       a += 1;  // equivalent to  a = a + 1;

       System.out.println(a);
    }
}
```

#### Output

```

6
```

In the above code, `a += 1` is equivalent to `a = a + 1`

_Example 2:_

#### Code

```java
class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
       int a = 10;
       int b = 11;
       a -= 2;  // equivalent to a = a - 2;
       b %= 3;  // equivalent to  b = b % 3;
       System.out.println(a);
       System.out.println(b);
    }
}
```

#### Output

```

8
2
```

> <details open>
> <summary>**Comparison with Python**</summary>
>
> #### Code
>
> ```python
> a = 10
> b = 11
> a -= 2
> b %= 3
> print(a)
> print(b)
> ```
>
> #### Output
>
> ```
>
> 8
> 2
> ```
>
> </details>

</Section>

<Section id="unary-operators">

## 2. Unary Operators

The unary operators are those that operate upon a single operand and produce a new value. We have learned some of the unary operators like _logical NOT_ (`!`) operator.

Let's learn few more unary operators like,

- Increment Operator
- Decrement Operator

### 2.1 Increment Operator

The **Increment Operator (`++`)** is an operator which is used to increment the value of a variable by 1, on which it is applied.

In Python, there is no increment operator.

Increment operator can be used in two ways:

- Prefix (++x)
- Postfix (x++)

**2.1.1 Prefix (++x)**

If an Increment operator is used in front of an operand, then it is called a Prefix.

In the prefix, the variable's value is incremented first, and then the updated value is used.

#### Syntax

```java
++variable;
```

#### Code

```java
class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int a = 10;
        ++a;            // a = 11
        int number = ++a; // a = 12, number = 12

       System.out.println("a = " + a);
       System.out.println("number = " + number);
    }
}

```

#### Output

```
a = 12
number = 12
```

In the above code, the statement `++a` increments the `a` value from 10 to 11.

In the statement `int number = ++a`, initially `a` will be incremented from 11 to 12, and then the updated value of `a` will be assigned to the `number`.

**2.1.2 Postfix (x++)**

If an Increment operator is used after an operand, then is called a Postfix.

In the postfix, the variable's value is first used for computing the result and then incremented.

#### Syntax

```java
variable++;
```

#### Code

```java
class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int a = 10;
        a++;              // a = 11
        int number = a++; // number = 11, a = 12

       System.out.println("a = " + a);
       System.out.println("number = " + number);
    }
}

```

#### Output

```
a = 12
number = 11
```

In the statement, `a++` the `a` value will be incremented from 10 to 11.

In the statement `int number = a++`, the variable `number` will be assigned the current value of `a` (11), and then `a` will be incremented from 11 to 12.

### 2.2 Decrement Operator

The Decrement operator is an operator which is used to decrease the value of the variable by 1, on which it is applied.

Similar to the increment operator, the decrement operator can also be used in two ways:

- Prefix (--x)
- Postfix (x--)

**2.2.1 Prefix (--x)**

Prefix decrement is similar to prefix increment, except that the variable value is decremented by one instead of being incremented.

#### Syntax

```java
--variable;
```

#### Code

```java
class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int a = 10;
        --a;            // a = 9
        int number = --a; // number = 8, a = 8

       System.out.println("a = " + a);
       System.out.println("number = " + number);
    }
}
```

#### Output

```
a = 8
number = 8
```

In the statement `--a`, the `a` value will be decremented from 10 to 9.

In the statement `int number = --a`, initially `a` will be decremented from 9 to 8, then the updated value of `a` will be assigned to the `number`.

**2.2.2 Postfix (x--)**

Postfix decrement is similar to postfix increment, except that the variable value is decremented by one instead of being incremented.

In the postfix, the current value of the variable in the expression is used, and later the variable value will be updated.

#### Syntax

```java
variable--;
```

#### Code

```java
class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int a = 10;
        a--;            // a = 9
        int number = a--; // number = 9, a = 8

       System.out.println("a = " + a);
       System.out.println("number = " + number);
    }
}

```

#### Output

```
a = 8
number = 9
```

In the statement `a--`, the `a` value will be decremented from 10 to 9.

In the statement `int number = a--`, the variable `number` will be assigned the current value of `a`, and then `a` will be decremented from 9 to 8.

**Key Points:**

- The increment and decrement operators should only be used on variables and not on constants.

- These operators will work on all primitive data types except `boolean`

- These operators will not work on the variables which are declared as `final`

**What if increment or decrement operators are used with constants?**

#### Code

```java|UGLY|ITALIC
class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int num = 5;

        num++;
        7++;

        System.out.println(num);
    }
}
```

#### Output

```
file.java:6: error: unexpected type
        7++;
        ^
  required: variable
  found:    value
1 error
```

An error will be thrown, as the increment and decrement operators should only be used on variables and not on constants.

#### Correct Code

```java
class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int num = 5;

        num++;

        System.out.println(num);
    }
}
```

#### Output

```

6
```

</Section>

<Section id="esc">

## 3. Escape Sequences

A character with a backslash `\` just before a character is called an escape character or escape sequence. As in Python, the escape characters have a special meaning to the compiler.

The escape sequence starts with a backslash.

**Most commonly used escape sequences include:**

- `\n` -> New Line
- `\t` -> Tab Space
- `\\` -> Backslash
- `\'` -> Single Quote
- `\"` -> Double Quote

Let's understand the uses of escape characters through the following example. Suppose, we have to print the following statement: `Hello user, "Welcome"`

#### Code

```java
class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello user, \"Welcome\"");
    }
}
```

#### Output

```

Hello user, "Welcome"
```

Let's see some more uses of the escape sequences with the following example:

#### Code

```java
class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello user, \"Welcome\".");  // Use of \"

        System.out.println("Hello, I am backslash \\.");  // Use of \\

        System.out.println("Hurray\tI am separated by a tab.");  // Use of \t

        System.out.println("Where are you? \nI am in a new line.");  // Use of \n
    }
}
```

#### Output

```
Hello user, "Welcome".
Hello, I am backslash \.
Hurray	I am separated by a tab.
Where are you?
I am in a new line.
```

In the above code,

- `\"`: inserts a double quote character in the text where it is used.
- `\\`: inserts a backslash character in the text where it is used.
- `\t`: inserts a tab in the text where it is used.
- `\n`: inserts a new line in the text where it is used.

> <details open>
> <summary>**Comparison with Python**</summary>
>
> #### Code
>
> ```python
> print("Hello user, \"Welcome\".")
> print("Hello, I am backslash \\.")
> print("Hurray\tI am separated by a tab.")
> print("Where are you? \nI am in a new line.")
> ```
>
> #### Output
>
> ```
> Hello user, "Welcome".
> Hello, I am backslash \.
> Hurray	I am separated by a tab.
> Where are you?
> I am in a new line.
> ```
>
> </details>

### 3.1 Possible Mistake

Printing the double quotes (`"`) without using escape character (`\`).

#### Incorrect Code

```java|UGLY|ITALIC
class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(""Hello World!"");
    }
}
```

#### Output

```
file.java:3: error: ')' expected
        System.out.println(""Hello World!"");
                             ^
file.java:3: error: ';' expected
        System.out.println(""Hello World!"");
                                        ^
2 errors
```

In the above code, the compiler needs to be told that double quotes (`"`) do not specify the start or end of a string, but instead are to be printed.

The following example prints the statements with double quotes (`"`).

#### Correct Code

```java
class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("\"Hello World!\"");
    }
}
```

#### Output

```

"Hello World!"
```

</Section>

<Section>

### Summary

- Compound assignment operators provide a shorter way to assign an expression to a variable.

- Increment Operator:

  - **Prefix (++x)**: the variable's value is incremented initially, and the updated value is used.
  - **Postfix (x++)**: the current value of the variable in the expression is used, and later the variable value will be incremented.

- Decrement Operator:

  - **Prefix (--x)**: the variable's value is decremented initially, and the updated value is used.
  - **Postfix (x--)**: the current value of the variable in the expression is used, and later the variable value will be decremented.

- Increment and Decrement operators can't be used with constants, variables declared as `final` and boolean variables.

- A character with a backslash `\` just before a character is called an escape character or escape sequence.

</Section>

# Arrays - Part 1
## Concepts Arrays Declaration of Array Creating and Initializing an Array Accessing Array Elements Array Index Out Of Bounds Exception Printing an Array Modifying Array Elements Creating an Array using `new` Keyword Length of an Array Iterating Over an Array Using for Loop Using for-each Loop Read & Store User Input in an Array
## Introduction Data structures allow us to store and organize data efficiently. This will allow us to easily access and perform operations on data. Java provides various data structures to store the data. In this unit, we'll learn the most commonly used data structure i.e., **Arrays**, and perform some basic operations on it. ## 1. Arrays In Java, an array is an object used to store the collection of data that are of similar data types (String, int, float, etc.) similar to lists in Python. In Java, the number of elements that an array can store is always fixed. ### 1.1 Declaration of Array The syntax for the declaration of an array is as follows: #### Syntax ```java dataType[] arrayName; ``` Here, - The `dataType` specifies the type of elements that can be stored in the array. It can be primitive data types (`int`, `char`, etc.) or non-primitive data types (`String`, etc.) - The `[]` after the `dataType`, differentiates the array from regular variable declarations. - `arrayName` is the name of the array variable. The declaration does not create an array, it simply tells the compiler that the `arrayName` variable will hold an array of the specified `dataType` Let's declare an array with the name `arr` that can store `int` type values. #### Example ```java class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { int[] arr; // declaring an Array } } ```
## 2. Creating and Initializing an Array We can declare, create and initialize an array in a single statement. The following is the syntax to create an array using array literals: #### Syntax ```java dataType[] arrayName = {value1, value2, value3, ...}; ``` Here, `value1`, `value2`, and etc are the values that will be stored in the array. These values should have the same data type as `dataType` The array literal `{value1, value2, ...}` creates the array and the reference of this array object is assigned to array variable `arrayName` _Example:_ #### Code ```java class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { int[] arr = {60, 25, 20, 15, 30}; // declaring, creating and initializing in a single statement } } ``` >
> **Comparison with Python** >
> > In Python, square braces `[]` are used instead of curly braces `{}` > > #### Code > > ```python > list_a = [60, 25, 20, 15, 30] > ``` > >
## 3. Accessing Array Elements Similar to Python, the array indices start from `0` i.e., the first element of an array is stored at index `0`, the second element of an array is stored at index `1`, and so on. If the size of an array is `n`, then the index of the last element of the array will be `n - 1` We can access the elements of an array using these index values. #### Syntax ```java arrayName[index]; ``` Here, the `index` value must lie between `0` and `n - 1` while `n` is the size of the array. #### Code ```java class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { int[] arr = {12, 4, 5, 2, 5}; System.out.println(arr[0]); System.out.println(arr[1]); System.out.println(arr[4]); } } ``` #### Output ``` 12 4 5 ``` >
> **Comparison with Python** > > #### Code > > ```python > list_a = [12, 4, 5, 2, 5] > print(list_a[0]) > print(list_a[1]) > print(list_a[4]) > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > 12 > 4 > 5 > ``` > >

### 3.1 Array Index Out Of Bounds Exception Accessing array elements with a negative index or, the index value greater than or equal to the size of the array throws an error. #### Incorrect Code ```java|UGLY|ITALIC class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { int[] arr = {12, 4, 5, 2, 5}; System.out.println(arr[5]); } } ``` #### Output ``` Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 5 out of bounds for length 5 at Main.main(file.java:5) ``` In the above code, the size of the `arr` array is `5`. So, the index values must lie between `0` and `4`. Since index `5` is outside the range, the error is thrown.
## 4. Printing an Array The `Arrays` class provides a method `toString()`, which can be used to print the array in Java. #### Syntax ```java Arrays.toString(arrayName); ``` #### Code ```java import java.util.Arrays; class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { int[] arr = {12, 4, 5, 2, 5}; System.out.println(Arrays.toString(arr)); } } ``` #### Output ``` [12, 4, 5, 2, 5] ``` >
> **Comparison with Python** >
> > In Python, we can directly print the arrays. > > #### Code > > ```python > list_a = [12, 4, 5, 2, 5] > print(list_a) > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > > [12, 4, 5, 2, 5] > ``` > >
## 5. Modifying Array Elements Similar to Python, arrays in Java are mutable. The array elements at any position can be modified but with the same data type. #### Code ```java import java.util.Arrays; class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { int[] arr = {12, 4, 5, 2, 5}; System.out.println("Initial Array: " + Arrays.toString(arr)); arr[0] = 56; arr[1] = 100; arr[4] = 21; System.out.println("After Modifying elements: " + Arrays.toString(arr)); } } ``` #### Output ``` Initial Array: [12, 4, 5, 2, 5] After Modifying elements: [56, 100, 5, 2, 21] ``` >
> **Comparison with Python** > > #### Code > > ```python > list_a = [12, 4, 5, 2, 5] > print(list_a) > list_a[0] = 56 > list_a[1] = 100 > list_a[4] = 21 > print(list_a) > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > [12, 4, 5, 2, 5] > [56, 100, 5, 2, 21] > ``` > >
### 5.1 Possible Mistake Updating elements in an array with different data type values. #### Incorrect Code ```java|UGLY|ITALIC import java.util.Arrays; class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { int[] arr = {12, 4, 5, 2, 5}; System.out.println(Arrays.toString(arr)); arr[3] = 10.6; System.out.println(Arrays.toString(arr)); } } ``` #### Output ``` file.java:9: error: incompatible types: possible lossy conversion from double to int arr[3] = 10.6; ^ 1 error ``` In the above code, we are trying to update the array `arr` at index `3` with `float` value. The array `arr` cannot store `float` values as it is declared with `int` data type. Hence, the error is thrown.
## 6. Creating an Array using a `new` Keyword We can also create the array using `new` keyword. Using this method, we can create an array of required length and later assign the values. The following is the syntax for creating an array using a `new` keyword: #### Syntax ```java dataType[] arrayName = new dataType[size]; ``` Here, the `size` specifies the number of elements we want to store in an array. _Example:_ #### Code ```java class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { int[] arr; // declaring an array arr = new int[3]; // allocating memory for 3 integer values } } ``` In the above code, the statement `arr = new int[3]` allocates memory for storing 3 `int` values. After creating a memory for the array, a default value of `0` is assigned to each element in the case of `byte`, `short`, `int`, or `long` type of array. For the `double` or `float` type of array, the default value is `0.0` is assigned. For the `String` array, the default value is `null`. In Java, `null` is a reserved word for literal values. It is a default value for every uninitialized non-primitive data type. ### 6.1 Assigning Values Let's assign the values to the array created using the `new` keyword. #### Code ```java import java.util.Arrays; class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { int[] arr; // declaring an array arr = new int[3]; // allocating memory for 3 integer values arr[0] = 56; arr[1] = 41; arr[2] = 25; System.out.println(Arrays.toString(arr)); } } ``` #### Output ``` [56, 41, 25] ```
## 7. Length of an Array Array length is the number of elements that an array can hold. In Java, we can find the array length by using the attribute `length`. #### Syntax ```java arrayName.length; ``` #### Code ```java class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { int[] arr = {12, 4, 5, 2, 5, 7}; int lengthOfArr = arr.length; System.out.println(lengthOfArr); } } ``` #### Output ``` 6 ``` >
> **Comparison with Python** >
> > In Python, we can find the length of the list using the built-in function `len()` > > #### Code > > ```python > list_a = [12, 4, 5, 2, 5, 7] > print(len(list_a)) > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > > 6 > ``` > >
## 8. Iterating Over an Array We can use loops to iterate over an array. ### 8.1 Using for Loop We can use `for` loop to access the array elements one after the other. #### Code ```java class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { int[] arr = {12, 4, 5}; int n = arr.length; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { System.out.println(arr[i]); } } } ``` #### Output ``` 12 4 5 ``` In the above code, `arr` array contains `3` elements. Hence, `n` = 3. The for loop will start iterating from `i = 0` - At i = 0, `System.out.println(arr[0])` will print value of 1st element of `arr` array. - At i = 1, `System.out.println(arr[1])` will print value of 2nd element of `arr` array. - At i = 2, `System.out.println(arr[2])` will print value of 3rd element of `arr` array. - At i = 3, loop test condition will fail .
### 8.2 Using for-each Loop Java consists of a `for-each` loop which can be used to iterate over an array. During iteration with the `for-each` loop, we will get array elements, but no index values. #### Syntax ```java for (dataType variableName : arrayName) { // body of loop } ``` Here, - `arrayName`: the name of an array - `variableName`: while iterating, each element of the array is assigned to this variable. - `dataType`: the data type of an array #### Code ```java class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { int[] arr = {12, 4, 5}; for(int element: arr){ System.out.println(element); } } } ``` #### Output ``` 12 4 5 ``` >
> **Comparison with Python** > > #### Code > > ```python > list_a = [12, 4, 5] > for item in list_a: > print(item) > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > 12 > 4 > 5 > ``` > >
## 9. Read & Store User Inputs in an Array Till now we have read user inputs and stored them in a variable. In order to read and store the user inputs in an array, initially, we need to create an array of the required length. Let's consider that the first input from the user indicates the required array length and the following inputs are the actual values to be stored in the array. #### Code ```java import java.util.*; class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in); int n = input.nextInt(); // n is the number of elements you want to store int[] arr = new int[n]; // declaring and creating an array for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { arr[i] = input.nextInt(); // reading inputs for array } System.out.println(Arrays.toString(arr)); input.close(); } } ``` #### Input ``` 7 34 45 19 90 2 100 56 ``` #### Output ``` [34, 45, 19, 90, 2, 100, 56] ``` In the above code, the first input `7` indicates the array length. The following space separated numbers are the actual values to be stored. In each iteration of the `for` loop, the `nextInt()` method reads a number and stores it in the array. >
> **Comparison with Python** > > #### Code > > ```python > list_a = [] > n = int(input()) > for i in range(0, n): > item = int(input()) > list_a.append(item) > print(list_a) > ``` > > #### Input > > ``` > 7 > 34 > 45 > 19 > 90 > 2 > 100 > 56 > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > > [34, 45, 19, 90, 2, 100, 56] > ``` > >
### Summary - In Java, the number of elements that an array can store is always fixed. - When an array is created using `new` keyword, the default values are assigned based on the data type of the array - `0` is assigned to each element in the case of `byte`, `short`, `int`, or `long` type of array - `0.0` is assigned for the `double` or `float` type of array. - `null` is assigned for the `String` array. - To print the array, the `toString()` method of the `Arrays` class can be used. - We can find the array length in Java by using the attribute `length` - While iterating with `for-each` loop, we will get array elements, but no index values.

# Arrays - Part 2
## Concepts Array Concatenation Array Slicing Multi-dimensional Array Two-dimensional Array Creating & Initializing a Two-dimensional Array Accessing Two-dimensional Array Elements Printing a Two-dimensional Array Creating a Two-dimensional Array using `new` Keyword Iterating Over a Two-dimensional Array Read & Store User Inputs in a Two-dimensional Array
## Introduction In the previous unit, we learned Arrays and performed some basic operations such as accessing and modifying them. In this unit, we'll learn to perform some more operations like concatenating two arrays and finding subarrays. We will also learn about Multi-dimensional arrays. ## 1. Array Concatenation Joining two arrays is called Array Concatenation. In Java, the `System` class contains a method named `arraycopy()` to concatenate two arrays. #### Syntax ```java System.arraycopy(array1, array1StartPosition, array2, array2StartPosition, noOfElements); ``` Here, - `array1`: is the name of the source array. - `array1StartPosition`: indicates from which position in the source array the elements need to be copied. - `array2`: is the name of the destination array - `array2StartPosition`: indicates to which position in the destination array the elements need to be added to. - `noOfElements`: is the number of array elements to be copied. #### Code ```java import java.util.Arrays; class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { int[] arr1 = {12, 4, 5, 2, 5}; int[] arr2 = {6, 10,11,6}; int arr1Len = arr1.length; // 5 int arr2Len = arr2.length; // 4 int[] concatenatedArr = new int[arr1Len + arr2Len]; // new int[9] System.arraycopy(arr1, 0, concatenatedArr, 0, arr1Len); System.out.println(Arrays.toString(concatenatedArr)); // Concatenated array after array1 elements is copied to it. System.arraycopy(arr2, 0, concatenatedArr, arr1Len, arr2Len); System.out.println(Arrays.toString(concatenatedArr)); } } ``` #### Output ``` [12, 4, 5, 2, 5, 0, 0, 0, 0] [12, 4, 5, 2, 5, 6, 10, 11, 6] ``` In the above code, - `concatenatedArr` has memory for storing **9** integer values. - `arraycopy(arr1, 0, concatenatedArr, 0, 5)` method tells the program to copy **5** elements of `arr1` starting from index **0** to `concatenatedArr` starting from index **0**. - The first output of the code shows the `concatenatedArr` after `arr1` elements are copied to it. - `arraycopy(arr2, 0, concatenatedArr, 5, 4)` method tells the program to copy **4** elements of `array2` starting from index **0** to `concatenatedArr` starting from index **5**. - The second output of the code shows the `concatenatedArr` after `arr2` elements are copied to it. >
> **Comparison with Python** >
> > In Python, we can use `+`operator to concatenate two lists. > > #### Code > > ```python > list1 = [12, 4, 5, 2, 5] > list2 = [6, 10, 11, 6] > concatenated_list = list1 + list2 > print(concatenated_list) > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > > [12, 4, 5, 2, 5, 6, 10, 11, 6] > ``` > >
## 2. Array Slicing Array slicing is a method of obtaining a subarray of an array. We can get the subarray from an array using `Arrays.copyOfRange()` method. #### Syntax ```java Arrays.copyOfRange(arrayName, startIndex, endIndex); ``` Here, - `arrayName` is the name of the array - The subarray starts from `startIndex` and stops at `endIndex - 1` - `endIndex` is not included in the subarray. #### Code ```java import java.util.Arrays; class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { int[] originalArr = { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 }; int startIndex = 2; int endIndex = 4; // copying the subarray from the original array to sliced array int[] slicedArr = Arrays.copyOfRange(originalArr, startIndex, endIndex); System.out.println(Arrays.toString(slicedArr)); } } ``` #### Output ``` [3, 4] ``` >
> **Comparison with Python** >
> In Python, with the help of the colon `:` operator, we can slice our list by specifying the start and end index. > > #### Code > > ```python > original_list = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] > sliced_list = original_list[2 : 4] > print(sliced_list) > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > > [3, 4] > ``` > >
## 3. Multi-dimensional Array A multi-dimensional array consists of an array of arrays. It is similar to the list of lists in Python. We can create `N` Dimensional arrays like 2D, 3D, etc. In the previous unit, we learned one-dimensional arrays. Now, let's look at the two-dimensional (2D) array. ### 3.1 Two-dimensional Array A two-dimensional array is the simplest form of a multidimensional array. A two-dimensional array is an array of arrays. In other words, a two-dimensional array is a collection of one-dimensional arrays. A two-dimensional array can be visualized as a matrix, which can be represented as a collection of rows and columns. ``` { {12, 24, 36}, {15, 30, 45}, {16, 32, 48} } ``` Here, - this two-dimensional array is a collection of **3** one-dimensional arrays - `rows` = number of one-dimensional arrays = **3** - `columns` = number of elements in each row = **3** - number of elements in two-dimensional array = (number of rows \* number of columns) = 3 \* 3 = 9 - As we know index in an array starts from **0**. So indexing of rows and columns also starts from **0**. - The array `{12, 24, 36}` is the 1st row of the two-dimensional array, for this complete row every element has its row index as **0** and the column index will lie from **0** to **2**. - **12** is stored at the 0th row and 0th column of the array - **24** is stored at the 0th row and 1st column of the array and so on for further elements for this row. - The array `{15, 30, 45}` is the 2nd row of a two-dimensional array, for this complete row every element has its row index as **1** and the column index will lie from **0** to **2**. - **15** is stored at the 1st row and 0th column of the array - **30** is stored at the 1st row and 1st column of the array and so on for further elements for this row. **3.1.1 Declaration of Two-dimensional Array** The syntax for the declaration of a two-dimensional array is as follows: #### Syntax ```java dataType[][] arrayName; ``` The syntax is similar to the one-dimensional array. The `[][]` after the `dataType`, differentiates it from the one-dimensional array and regular variable declarations. The number of square braces (`[]`) indicates the dimensions. For example, three-dimensional (3D) array is declared as `dataType[][][] arrayName` #### Code ```java class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { int[][] arr; // declaring a two-dimensional array } } ``` The `arr` is a two-dimensional array that can store elements of type `int`.
## 4. Creating & Initializing a Two-dimensional Array Using array literals we can declare, create and initialize a two-dimensional array in a single statement. The following is the syntax to create a two-dimensional array using array literals: #### Syntax ```java dataType[][] arrayName = { {value00, value01, ...}, {value10, value11, ...}, {value20, value21, ...}, ...}; ``` Here, - `value00`: is the value that will be stored at the 0th row and 0th column of the array `arr`. - `value01`: is the value that will be stored at the 0th row and 1st column of the array `arr` and so on. _Example:_ #### Code ```java class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { int[][] arr = { {45, 42}, {11, 34}, {56, 79} }; } } ``` In the above code, - The number of rows is **3** - The number of columns is **2** - 0th row and 0th column of array `arr` contain the value **45**. - 0th row and 1st column of array `arr` contain the value **42**. - 1st row and 0th column of array `arr` contain the value **11** and so on.
>
> **Comparison with Python** > > #### Code > > ```python > data = [ [45, 42], [11, 34] , [56, 79] ] > > ``` > >
## 5. Accessing Two-dimensional Array Elements We use row and column indices to access a particular element from a two-dimensional array. #### Syntax ```java arrayName[rowNo][colNo]; ``` #### Code ```java class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { int[][] arr = {{12, 4, 5}, {16, 18, 20}}; System.out.println(arr[0][0]); System.out.println(arr[1][1]); System.out.println(arr[1][2]); } } ``` #### Output ``` 12 18 20 ``` >
> **Comparison with Python** > > #### Code > > ```python > data = [[12, 4, 5], [16, 18, 20]] > print(data[0][0]) > print(data[1][1]) > print(data[1][2]) > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > 12 > 18 > 20 > ``` > >
## 6. Printing a Two-dimensional Array To print a two-dimensional array or any multi-dimensional array, we can use `Arrays.deepToString()` method. #### Code ```java import java.util.Arrays; class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { int[][] arr = { {12, 4, 5}, {16, 18, 20} }; System.out.println(Arrays.deepToString(arr)); } } ``` #### Output ``` [[12, 4, 5], [16, 18, 20]] ``` >
> **Comparison with Python** > > #### Code > > ```python > data = [ [12, 4, 5], [16, 18, 20] ] > print(data) > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > > [[12, 4, 5], [16, 18, 20]] > ``` > >
## 7. Creating a Two-dimensional Array using `new` Keyword We can also create the two-dimensional array using a `new` keyword. Using this method, we can create a two-dimensional array of the required number of rows and columns and later assign the values. The following is the syntax for creating an array using a `new` keyword: #### Syntax ```java dataType[][] arrayName = new dataType[rows][columns]; ``` Here, - `arrayName`: name of the two-dimensional array. - `rows`: specifies the number of rows. - `columns`: specifies the number of columns. _Example_: Let's create a two-dimensional array with the name `arr`: #### Code ```java class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { int[][] arr; // declaring an array arr = new int[2][2]; // allocating memory for arr } } ``` In the above code, the statement `arr = new int[2][2]` allocates memory for storing 2\*2 = 4 `int` values. After creating a memory for the two-dimensional array, a default value of **0** is assigned to each element as the array is of `int` data type. ### 7.1 Assigning Values Let's assign the values to the two-dimensional array created using the `new` keyword. #### Code ```java import java.util.Arrays; class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { int[][] arr; // declaring an array arr = new int[2][2]; // allocating memory for arr // assigning values to first row arr[0][0] = 12; arr[0][1] = 46; // assigning values to second row arr[1][0] = 61; arr[1][1] = 90; System.out.println(Arrays.deepToString(arr)); } } ``` #### Output ``` [[12, 46], [61, 90]] ```
## 8. Iterating Over a Two-dimensional Array We can use nested loops to iterate over a two-dimensional array. ### 8.1 Using nested for Loop We can use nested `for` loops to iterate over a two-dimensional array. #### Code ```java class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { int[][] arr = { {12, 45, 54}, {16, 18, 20}, {23, 78, 53} }; int rows = arr.length; int cols = arr[0].length; for (int i = 0; i < rows; i++) { for (int j = 0; j < cols; j++) { System.out.println("arr[" + i +"][" + j + "]: " + arr[i][j]); } } } } ``` #### Output ``` arr[0][0]: 12 arr[0][1]: 45 arr[0][2]: 54 arr[1][0]: 16 arr[1][1]: 18 arr[1][2]: 20 arr[2][0]: 23 arr[2][1]: 78 arr[2][2]: 53 ``` In the above code, - The array `arr` contains 3 rows and each row contains 3 elements. Hence, rows = 3 and cols = 3. - The outer for loop iterates from `i = 0` to `i = 2`, this loop handles the row number. - The inner for loop iterates from `j = 0` to `j = 2`, this loop handles the column number. - At `i = 0`, and - `j = 0`, `System.out.println(arr[0][0])` will print the value of 0th row and 0th column value of the array `arr`. Similarly, it runs till `j = 2`. - `j = 3`, the inner loop test condition fails and control goes to the outer loop now. Similarly, the corresponding row values will be printed for `i = 1`, and `1 = 2` >
> **Comparison with Python** > > #### Code > > ```python > data = [[12, 45, 54], [16, 18, 20], [23, 78, 53] ] > for i in range(len(data)): > for j in range(len(data[i])): > print(data[i][j]) > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > 12 > 45 > 54 > 16 > 18 > 20 > 23 > 78 > 53 > ``` > >
## 9. Read & Store User Inputs in a Two-dimensional Array In the previous unit, we learned to read and store user inputs in a one-dimensional array. Similar to the one-dimensional array, initially, we need to create an array (two-dimensional array) to store the user inputs. We have used `for` loop to read user inputs in a one-dimensional array. For a two-dimensional array, we need to use nested `for` loops. We need to get the number of rows and columns required to create the two-dimensional array. Let's consider that the first two numbers indicate the rows and columns, followed by the actual values to be stored. #### Code ```java import java.util.*; class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in); int rows = input.nextInt(); // reads the number of rows. int cols = input.nextInt(); // reads the number of columns. int[][] arr = new int[rows][cols]; // creating a two-dimensional arrray for (int i = 0; i < rows; i++) { for (int j = 0; j < cols; j++) { arr[i][j] = input.nextInt(); // reading and storing user inputs in array } } System.out.println(Arrays.deepToString(arr)); input.close(); } } ``` #### Input 1 ``` 2 2 16 64 32 128 ``` #### Input 2 ``` 2 2 16 64 32 128 ``` #### Output ``` [[16, 64], [32, 128]] ``` The above code works the same for **Input 1** and **Input 2**. >
> **Comparison with Python** > > #### Code > > ```python > rows = int(input()) > cols = int(input()) > data = [] > for i in range(rows): > list_a = [] > for j in range(cols): > item = int(input()) > list_a.append(item) > data.append(list_a) > print(data) > ``` > > #### Input > > ``` > 2 > 2 > 16 > 64 > 32 > 128 > ``` > > Output > > ``` > > [[16, 64], [32, 128]] > ``` > >
### Summary - Array Concatenation, - We can use the `System.arraycopy()` method to concatenate arrays. - Array Slicing, - We can use the `Arrays.copyOfRange()` method for array slicing. - Multi-dimensional arrays, - A multi-dimensional array is an array of arrays. - A two-dimensional array will contain rows and columns. - To print elements in the multi-dimensional arrays, we can use the `Arrays.deepToString()` method. - We can use nested loops to iterate over a multi-dimensional array.

# ArrayLists - Part 2
## Concepts ArrayList Concatenation ArrayList Slicing Converting Array to ArrayList Converting ArrayList to Array Comparison between ArrayList and Array
## Introduction In the previous unit, we learned ArrayLists and how to perform basic operations on them, such as creating, accessing, etc. In this unit, we'll learn some more operations such as concatenation, slicing, etc on ArrayLists. We will also learn to convert Arrays to ArrayLists and vice-versa. ## 1. ArrayList Concatenation The `addAll()` method is used to concatenate two ArrayLists. This method appends the second ArrayList to the end of the first ArrayList. It modifies the existing ArrayList. #### Syntax ```java arrList1.addAll(arrList2); ``` The concatenated ArrayList is stored in `arrList1` #### Code ```java import java.util.ArrayList; class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { ArrayList arrList1 = new ArrayList<>(); arrList1.add(5); arrList1.add(10); arrList1.add(15); arrList1.add(20); System.out.println("arrList1: " + arrList1); // [5, 10, 15, 20] ArrayList arrList2 = new ArrayList<>(); arrList2.add(25); arrList2.add(30); arrList2.add(35); arrList2.add(40); System.out.println("arrList2: " + arrList2); // [25, 30, 35, 40] arrList1.addAll(arrList2); System.out.println("arrList1 after concatenation: " + arrList1); // [5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40] } } ``` #### Output ``` arrList1: [5, 10, 15, 20] arrList2: [25, 30, 35, 40] arrList1 after concatenation: [5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40] ``` >
> **Comparison with Arrays** > >
> > In Arrays, the `arraycopy()` method is used to concatenate Arrays. A new Array is created to store the concatenated Array. > > #### Code > > ```java > import java.util.Arrays; > > class Main { > public static void main(String[] args) { > int[] arr1 = {5, 10, 15, 20}; > int[] arr2 = {25, 30, 35,40}; > > int arr1Len = arr1.length; // 4 > int arr2Len = arr2.length; // 4 > > int[] concatenatedArr = new int[arr1Len + arr2Len]; // new int[8] > > System.arraycopy(arr1, 0, concatenatedArr, 0, arr1Len); > System.arraycopy(arr2, 0, concatenatedArr, arr1Len, arr2Len); > > > System.out.println("arr1: " + Arrays.toString(arr1)); // [5, 10, 15, 20] > System.out.println("arr2: " + Arrays.toString(arr2)); // [25, 30, 35, 40] > System.out.println("concatenatedArr: " + Arrays.toString(concatenatedArr)); // [5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40] > } > } > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > arr1: [5, 10, 15, 20] > arr2: [25, 30, 35, 40] > concatenatedArr: [5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40] > ``` > >
## 2. ArrayList Slicing The `subList()` method is used for slicing of ArrayLists. It works similar to the `copyOfRange()` method in Arrays. #### Syntax ```java arrList.subList(startIndex, endIndex); ``` Here, - the slicing starts from the `startIndex` and stops at the `endIndex` - `endIndex` is not included in the slice. It returns a `List`, which is an _interface_. The `ArrayList` constructor can be used to convert the `List` to an `ArrayList` by passing it as an argument to the constructor of `ArrayList`. > We will learn about **Interfaces** later in the course. #### Code ```java import java.util.ArrayList; class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { ArrayList arrList = new ArrayList<>(); arrList.add(5); arrList.add(10); arrList.add(15); arrList.add(20); ArrayList subArrList = new ArrayList<>(arrList.subList(1, 3)); // [10, 15] System.out.println(subArrList); } } ``` #### Output ``` [10, 15] ``` In the above code, - The ArrayList `arrList` is declared and initialized. - We have passed an argument `arrList.subList(1, 3)` to the ArrayList constructor to convert the `List` returned by the `subList()` method to an `ArrayList`. >
> **Comparison with Arrays** > > #### Code > > ```java > import java.util.Arrays; > > class Main { > public static void main(String[] args) { > int[] arr = { 5, 10, 15, 20}; > int startIndex = 1; > int endIndex = 3; > > int[] subArr = Arrays.copyOfRange(arr, startIndex, endIndex); // [10, 15] > > System.out.println(Arrays.toString(subArr)); > } > } > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > > [10, 15] > ``` > >
## 3. Converting Array to ArrayList The `asList()` method from the `Arrays` class is used to convert an Array to an ArrayList by passing it as an argument to the constructor of ArrayList. The `asList()` method returns a `List`. #### Syntax ```java Arrays.asList(arr); ``` Let's look at few examples for converting Arrays to ArrayLists. _Example 1:_ #### Code ```java import java.util.*; class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { String[] sportsArr = {"Basketball", "Cricket", "Football"}; System.out.println("Type of sportsArr: " + sportsArr.getClass().getSimpleName()); ArrayList sportsArrList = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(sportsArr)); // converting Array to ArrayList System.out.println("sportsArrList: " + sportsArrList); // [Basketball", "Cricket", "Football] System.out.println("Type of sportsArrList: " + sportsArrList.getClass().getSimpleName()); } } ``` #### Output ``` Type of sportsArr: String[] sportsArrList: [Basketball, Cricket, Football] Type of sportsArrList: ArrayList ``` In the above code, - The Array `sportsArr` is declared and initialized. - An ArrayList with the name `sportsArrList` was created - We have passed an argument `Arrays.asList(sportsArr)` to the ArrayList constructor to convert the `List` returned by the `asList()` method to an `ArrayList`. _Example 2:_ #### Code ```java import java.util.*; class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { Integer[] agesArr = {5, 10, 15}; System.out.println("Type of agesArr: " + agesArr.getClass().getSimpleName()); ArrayList agesArrList= new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(agesArr)); // converting Array to ArrayList. System.out.println("agesArrList: " + agesArrList); // [5, 10, 15] System.out.println("Type of agesArrList: " + agesArrList.getClass().getSimpleName()); } } ``` #### Output ``` Type of agesArr: Integer[] agesArrList: [5, 10, 15] Type of agesArrList: ArrayList ``` In the above code, - The Array `agesArr` is declared and initialized. - ArrayLists can only store objects and not primitive data types. Hence, to declare `agesArr`, we have used the wrapper class `Integer` and not the `int`. - We have passed an argument `Arrays.asList(agesArr)` to the ArrayList constructor to convert the `List` returned by the `asList()` method to an `ArrayList`.
## 4. Converting ArrayList to Array The `toArray()` method is used to convert ArrayList to Array. #### Syntax ```java arrList.toArray(arr); ``` Here, - `arrList` is an ArrayList - `toArray()` is the method of the `ArrayList` class - `arr` is an array, to which the `arrList` elements are copied. #### Code ```java import java.util.*; class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { ArrayList agesArrList = new ArrayList<>(); agesArrList.add(5); agesArrList.add(10); agesArrList.add(15); System.out.println("Type of agesArrList: " + agesArrList.getClass().getSimpleName()); Integer[] agesArr = new Integer[agesArrList.size()]; // new Integer[3] agesArrList.toArray(agesArr); System.out.println("agesArr: " + Arrays.toString(agesArr)); // [5, 10, 15] System.out.println("Type of agesArr: " + agesArr.getClass().getSimpleName()); } } ``` #### Output ``` Type of agesArrList: ArrayList agesArr: [5, 10, 15] Type of agesArr: Integer[] ``` In the above code, - The ArrayList `agesArrList` is declared and initialized. - ArrayLists can only store objects and not primitive data types. Hence, to declare `agesArr`, we have used the wrapper class `Integer` and not the `int` to store the elements from the `agesArrList`.
## 5. Comparison between Array and ArrayList | Base | Arrays | ArrayList | | :------------------: | :------------------------------------------------------------: | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------: | | Size | Arrays are static and have a fixed length | ArrayLists can have dynamic sizes and can increase or decrease accordingly | | Nature of data types | Primitive data types can be added directly | Primitive data types cannot be added directly, rather they are added indirectly using wrapper classes | | Speed | Arrays are faster because they are static and have fixed sizes | ArrayLists are relatively slow due to their dynamic nature |
### Summary - ArrayList methods: - `addAll()` method is used for concatenation of ArrayLists. - `subList()` method is used to obtain the portion of an ArrayList. - Conversion between Arrays and ArrayLists: - `Arrays.asList()` method is used to convert `Array` to `ArrayList` - `toArray()` method of `ArrayList` is used to convert `ArrayList` into an `Array`

# ArrayList Methods
## Concepts Finding Index of an Element Finding Frequency of an Element Sorting an ArrayList Ascending Order Descending Order
## Introduction Previously, we learned to perform CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) operations as well as operations like concatenation, slicing, etc on ArrayLists. In this unit, we'll learn some more operations such as finding the index of an element and sorting the ArrayLists, etc. ## 1. Finding Index of an Element The `indexOf()` method returns the index of the first occurrence of the specified element in the ArrayList. If the ArrayList does not contain the element, `-1` is returned. As ArrayLists store elements as objects, the search parameter(i.e, the element to be searched) must be given as an object. #### Syntax ```java arrList.indexOf(obj); ``` The `indexOf()` method compares the value of a given object with the value of each object in the ArrayList. _Example 1:_ #### Code ```java import java.util.*; class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { ArrayList arrList = new ArrayList<>(); arrList.add(3); arrList.add(6); arrList.add(2); arrList.add(1); System.out.println(arrList); int index = arrList.indexOf((Integer)6); // finding index of 6. System.out.println(index); } } ``` #### Output ``` [3, 6, 2, 1] 1 ``` In the above code, we have used the wrapper class `Integer` to type cast `6` into an object.
>
> > **Comparison with Python** > >
> > Similar to `indexOf()` in Java, Python has a method called `index()` > > #### Code > > ```python > list_a = [3, 6, 2, 1] > print(list_a) > item_index = list_a.index(6) > print(item_index) > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > [3, 6, 2, 1] > 1 > ``` > >

_Example 2:_ The `indexOf()` method compares values and not the reference values of the objects. #### Code ```java import java.util.*; class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { ArrayList arrList = new ArrayList<>(); String str1 = "A"; String str2 = "B"; String str3 = new String("A"); arrList.add(str1); arrList.add(str2); arrList.add(str3); System.out.println(arrList); int index = arrList.indexOf(str3); // finding index of "A". System.out.println(index); } } ``` #### Output ``` [A, B, A] 0 ``` In the above code, even though we have provided the new reference of string `A` i.e.,`str3` to the `indexOf()` method, it compared the values instead of references and returned the index as `0`. >
> > **Comparison with Python** > > #### Code > > ```python > list_a = ['A', 'B', 'A'] > print(list_a) > item_index = list_a.index('A') > print(item_index) > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > ['A', 'B', 'A'] > 0 > ``` > >

_Example 3:_ If the ArrayList does not contain the element, `-1` is returned. #### Code ```java import java.util.*; class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { ArrayList arrList = new ArrayList<>(); arrList.add(3); arrList.add(6); arrList.add(2); arrList.add(1); System.out.println(arrList); int index = arrList.indexOf((Integer)5); // finding index of 5, which is not present in the arrList System.out.println(index); // Returns -1 , as 5 is not present in the arrList. } } ``` #### Output ``` [3, 6, 2, 1] -1 ``` >
> > **Comparison with Python** > >
> > Python throws an error upon searching for an item which is not present in the list. > > #### Code > > ```python > list_a = [3, 6, 2, 1] > print(list_a) > item_index = list_a.index(5) # asking to find the index of item not in the list . > print(item_index) > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > [3, 6, 2, 1] > > > Traceback (most recent call last): > File "main.py", line 3, in > item_index = list_a.index(5) # asking to find the index of an item not in the list . > ValueError: 5 is not in list > ``` > >

## 2. Finding Frequency of an Element The `Collections.frequency()` method is used to find the frequency with which an element occurs in the given ArrayList. The `java.util` package contains the `Collections` class. #### Syntax ```java Collections.frequency(arrList, obj); ``` Here, - `arrList` is an ArrayList - `obj` is the object/element whose frequency is to be found. #### Code ```java import java.util.*; class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { ArrayList arrList = new ArrayList<>(); arrList.add(3); arrList.add(6); arrList.add(2); arrList.add(1); arrList.add(2); System.out.println(arrList); // Find the frequency of element 2 int frequency = Collections.frequency(arrList, (Integer)2); System.out.println(frequency); } } ``` #### Output ``` [3, 6, 2, 1, 2] 2 ``` In the above code, we have used the wrapper class `Integer` to type cast `2` into an object. >
> > **Comparison with Python** > >
> > Similar to `Collections.frequency()` in Java, Python has a method called `count()` > > #### Code > > ```python > list_a = [3, 6, 2, 1, 2] > print(list_a) > items_count = list_a.count(2) > print(items_count) > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > [3, 6, 2, 1, 2] > 2 > ``` > >
## 3. Sorting an ArrayList The `Collections.sort()` method can be used to sort the given ArrayList in two different ways 1. Ascending order 2. Descending order This method modifies the given ArrayList. ### 3.1 Ascending Order Let's look at sorting an ArrayList in ascending order. #### Syntax ```java Collections.sort(arrList); ``` _Example 1:_ #### Code ```java import java.util.*; class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { ArrayList arrList = new ArrayList<>(); arrList.add(3); arrList.add(6); arrList.add(2); arrList.add(1); System.out.println(arrList); // Sorting the ArrayList in ascending order Collections.sort(arrList); System.out.println(arrList); } } ``` #### Output ``` [3, 6, 2, 1] [1, 2, 3, 6] ```
>
> >
> > Similar to `Collections.sort()` in Java, Python has a method called `sort()` > > > **Comparison with Python** > > #### Code > > ```python > list_a = [3, 6, 2, 1] > print(list_a) > list_a.sort() > print(list_a) > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > [3, 6, 2, 1] > [1, 2, 3, 6] > ``` > >

_Example 2:_ #### Code ```java import java.util.*; class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { ArrayList arrList = new ArrayList<>(); arrList.add('E'); arrList.add('K'); arrList.add('B'); arrList.add('O'); System.out.println(arrList) ; // Sorting the ArrayList in ascending order. Collections.sort(arrList) ; System.out.println(arrList) ; } } ``` #### Output ``` [E, K, B, O] [B, E, K, O] ```
>
>**Comparison with Python** > > #### Code > > ```python > list_a = ['E', 'K', 'B', 'O'] > print(list_a) > list_a.sort() > print(list_a) > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` >['E', 'K', 'B', 'O'] >['B', 'E', 'K', 'O'] > ``` > >

### 3.2 Descending Order An ArrayList can be sorted in descending order by passing the argument `Collection.reverseOrder()` to the `Collections.sort()` method. #### Syntax ```java Collections.sort(arrList, Collections.reverseOrder()); ``` Here, the `arrList` must be the first argument, `Collection.reverseOrder()` must be the second argument. _Example 1:_ #### Code ```java import java.util.*; class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { ArrayList arrList = new ArrayList<>(); arrList.add(3); arrList.add(6); arrList.add(2); arrList.add(1); System.out.println(arrList); // Sorting the ArrayList in descending order Collections.sort(arrList, Collections.reverseOrder()) ; System.out.println(arrList); } } ``` #### Output ``` [3, 6, 2, 1] [6, 3, 2, 1] ```
>
> > **Comparison with Python** > >
> > In Python, we send the keyword argument as `sort(reverse = True)` > > #### Code > > ```python > list_a = [3, 6, 2, 1] > print(list_a) > list_a.sort(reverse = True) > print(list_a) > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > [3, 6, 2, 1] > [6, 3, 2, 1] > ``` > >

_Example 2:_ #### Code ```java import java.util.*; class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { ArrayList arrList = new ArrayList<>(); arrList.add("Bryant"); arrList.add("Wade"); arrList.add("Garnett"); arrList.add("Rose"); System.out.println(arrList); // Sorting the ArrayList in descending order Collections.sort(arrList, Collections.reverseOrder()) ; System.out.println(arrList); } } ``` #### Output ``` [Bryant, Wade, Garnett, Rose] [Wade, Rose, Garnett, Bryant] ```
>
> > **Comparison with Python** > > #### Code > > ```python > list_a = ['Bryant', 'Wade', 'Garnett', 'Rose'] > print(list_a) > list_a.sort(reverse = True) > print(list_a) > ``` > > #### Output > > ``` > ['Bryant', 'Wade', 'Garnett', 'Rose'] > ['Wade', 'Rose', 'Garnett', 'Bryant'] > ``` > >

### Summary - The `indexOf()` method returns the index of the first occurrence of the specified element in the ArrayList. If the ArrayList does not contain the element, -1 is returned. - The `Collections.frequency()` method returns the frequency with which an element occurs in the given ArrayList. - Sorting of ArrayLists: - `Collections.sort()`: It sorts the ArrayList in ascending order. - `Collections.sort(arrList, Collections.reverseOrder())`: It sorts the ArrayList in descending order.

## Introduction

In the previous unit, we learned Arrays & ArrayLists. In this unit, we'll understand the behaviour of Arrays and ArrayLists with mutable and immutable objects.

## Modifying Array & ArrayList - 1

Let's consider that `arr1` and `arr2` are two arrays.

When the array `arr2` is assigned with an existing array `arr1`, both the array variables `arr1` and `arr2` will refer to the same array.

The same applies to ArrayList.

Let's understand this with some examples:

**Modifying Array**

#### Code

```java
import java.util.Arrays;

class Main {
	public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] arr1 = {34, 45, 19, 21};
        int[] arr2 = arr1;
        arr2[1] = 100;
        arr1[3] = 76;

		System.out.println(Arrays.toString(arr1));
		System.out.println(Arrays.toString(arr2));
	}
}
```

#### Output

```
[34, 100, 19, 76]
[34, 100, 19, 76]
```

In the above code, the `arr2` points to the array referenced by `arr1`. Hence, if we modify the array elements using any of the arrays (`arr1` or `arr2`), then it will be reflected in the other array too.

**Modifying ArrayList**

#### Code

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;

class Main {
	public static void main(String[] args) {
        ArrayList<Integer> arrList1  = new ArrayList<>();

        arrList1.add(34);
        arrList1.add(45);
        arrList1.add(19);
        arrList1.add(21);

        ArrayList<Integer> arrList2 = arrList1;

        arrList2.set(1, 100);
        arrList2.set(3, 76);

        System.out.println(arrList1);
        System.out.println(arrList2);
	}
}
```

#### Output

```
[34, 100, 19, 76]
[34, 100, 19, 76]
```

In the above code, similar to Arrays, if we modify the ArrayList elements using any of the ArrayLists (`arrList1` or `arrList2`), then it will be reflected in the other ArrayList too.

> <details open>
> <summary>**Comparison with Python**</summary>
>
> #### Code
>
> ```python
> list_a = [34, 45, 19, 21]
> list_b = list_a
> list_b[1] = 100
> list_a[3] = 76
> print(list_a)
> print(list_b)
> ```
>
> #### Output
>
> ```
> [34, 100, 19, 76]
> [34, 100, 19, 76]
> ```
>
> </details>

</Section>

<Section id="3a">

## Modifying Array & ArrayList - 2

When `arr1` and `arr2` are referring to the same array and `arr2` is assigned a new array, then `arr2` refers to the new array and `arr1` will be referring to the old array.

The same applies to ArrayList.

Let's understand this with some examples:

**Modifying Array**

#### Code

```java
import java.util.Arrays;

class Main {
	public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] arr1 = {34, 45, 19, 21};
        int[] arr2 = arr1;

        arr2 = new int[4];

	    System.out.println(Arrays.toString(arr1));
	    System.out.println(Arrays.toString(arr2));
	}
}
```

#### Output

```
[34, 45, 19, 21]
[0, 0, 0, 0]
```

In the above code, initially, both `arr1` and `arr2` are referencing the same array.

After the statement `arr2 = new int[4]`, a new array for storing 4 `int` values is created and `arr2` contains the reference of this new array.

**Modifying ArrayList**

#### Code

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;

class Main {
	public static void main(String[] args) {
        ArrayList<Integer> arrList1  = new ArrayList<>();

        arrList1.add(34);
        arrList1.add(45);
        arrList1.add(19);
        arrList1.add(21);

        ArrayList<Integer> arrList2 = arrList1;

        arrList2 = new ArrayList<>();

        System.out.println(arrList1);
        System.out.println(arrList2);
	}
}
```

#### Output

```
[34, 45, 19, 21]
[]
```

In the above code, initially, both `arrList1` and `arrList2` are referencing the same ArrayList.

After the statement `arrList2 = new ArrayList<>()`, a new ArrayList is created and `arrList2` contains the reference of the new ArrayList.

> <details open>
> <summary>**Comparison with Python**</summary>
>
> #### Code
>
> ```python
> list_a = [34, 45, 19, 21]
> list_b = list_a
> list_b = [6, 7, 8, 9]
> print(list_a)
> print(list_b)
> ```
>
> #### Output
>
> ```
> [34, 45, 19, 21]
> [6, 7, 8, 9]
> ```
>
> </details>

</Section>

<Section id="4a">

## Modifying Array & ArrayList - 3

Updating immutable objects will not affect the values in an array, as the reference of the immutable object will be changed.

The same applies to ArrayList.

Let's understand this with some examples:

**Modifying Array**

#### Code

```java
import java.util.Arrays;

class Main {
	public static void main(String[] args) {
	    String name = "John";
	    String[] namesArr = {name, "Smith", "Mike"};

	    System.out.println(Arrays.toString(namesArr));

		name = "John Martin";

	    System.out.println(Arrays.toString(namesArr));
	}
}
```

#### Output

```
[John, Smith, Mike]
[John, Smith, Mike]
```

In the above code, we can see that assigning a new value to the variable `name` did not affect the `namesArr`.

**Modifying ArrayList**

#### Code

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;

class Main {
	public static void main(String[] args) {
        ArrayList<String> arrList1  = new ArrayList<>();

        String name = "John";

        arrList1.add(name);
        arrList1.add("Smith");
        arrList1.add("Mike");

        System.out.println(arrList1);

        name = "John Martin";

        System.out.println(arrList1);
    }
}
```

#### Output

```
[John, Smith, Mike]
[John, Smith, Mike]
```

> <details open>

<Section id="5a">

## Modifying Array & ArrayList - 4

Updating mutable objects will affect the elements in the array.

The same applies to ArrayList.

#### Code

```java
import java.util.Arrays;

class Main {
	public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] arr1 = {34, 45, 19, 21};
        int[] arr2 = {42, 152, 737, 2, 79};
        int[][] arr3 = {arr1, arr2};

        System.out.println(Arrays.deepToString(arr3));

        arr1[1] = 65;
        arr2[4] = 41;

        System.out.println(Arrays.deepToString(arr3));
	}
}
```

#### Output

```
[[34, 45, 19, 21], [42, 152, 737, 2, 79]]
[[34, 65, 19, 21], [42, 152, 737, 2, 41]]
```

In the above code, `arr3` is a two-dimensional array storing two one-dimensional arrays(`arr1` and `arr2`).

When `arr1` and `arr2` are modified, it affected the `arr3`

> <details open>
> <summary>**Comparison with Python**</summary>
>
> #### Code
>
> ```python
> list_a = [34, 45, 19, 21]
> list_b = [42, 152, 737, 2, 79]
> list_c = [list_a, list_b]
> print(list_c)
> list_a[1] = 65
> list_b[4] = 41
> print(list_c)
> ```
>

>
> ```
> [[34, 45, 19, 21], [42, 152, 737, 2, 79]]
> [[34, 65, 19, 21], [42, 152, 737, 2, 41]]
> ```
>
> </details>

</Section>

### Summary

- When the array `arr2` is assigned with an existing array `arr1` both the array variables `arr1` and `arr2` will be referring to the same array. if we modify the array elements using any of the arrays (`arr1` or `arr2`), then it will be reflected in the other array too.

- Updating immutable objects will not affect the values in an array, as the reference of the immutable object will be changed.

- Updating mutable objects will affect the values in the array.
